questions.passage: Captain Vera Okafor had crossed the Atlantic seven times. She knew every mood of the sea — its green summer calm, its gray autumn restlessness, its winter fury. When her first mate pointed at a thin line of clouds on the horizon and said it was nothing, she shook her head. She had seen those clouds before. She ordered the crew to secure the cargo and reduce sail. Twelve hours later, when the storm struck with hurricane-force winds, the ship was ready.
questions.text: Which quote from the passage BEST supports the inference that Captain Okafor's experience saved the ship?
options: 'She had crossed the Atlantic seven times.'
'Her first mate said it was nothing.'
'She had seen those clouds before' and 'the ship was ready' when the storm struck.
'She knew every mood of the sea — its green summer calm.'
questions.explanation: The combination of 'She had seen those clouds before' — showing she recognized the warning sign — and the ship being fully ready when the storm struck directly supports that her experience made the difference.

questions.passage: All her life, Nadia had been told she was too quiet to be a leader. In student council elections, she barely spoke during debates while others shouted over each other. But every student she ever talked to one-on-one trusted her completely. When the council faced a crisis — a budget cut that threatened the school garden — it was Nadia who quietly spoke with each board member individually, listened to their concerns, and crafted a compromise that saved the garden. The loudest voice in the room, she had discovered, is not always the most powerful one.
questions.text: What is the theme of this passage?
options: Student government is more important than people think.
School gardens should be protected from budget cuts.
Quiet, thoughtful leadership can be more effective than loud assertiveness.
Students should always speak up during debates.
questions.explanation: Nadia succeeds not by shouting but by listening and building trust one person at a time; the story's conclusion states the loudest voice is not always the most powerful, directly expressing the theme.

questions.passage: Chapter 1 introduced twins Eli and Sofia, who both wanted to win the science fair. Eli worked quickly, testing many ideas but rarely finishing any of them. Sofia worked slowly, spending two weeks on a single experiment with careful measurements. In Chapter 4, the judges awarded Sofia first place for the precision of her data. Eli congratulated her, then quietly started a new notebook — this time, he chose just one idea and wrote 'Day 1' at the top.
questions.text: How are Eli and Sofia different, and how does that difference lead to the story's outcome?
options: Eli is smarter than Sofia, but she worked harder.
Sofia works carefully and precisely; Eli jumps between ideas — this difference leads Sofia to win, and it changes Eli's approach.
Both twins work the same way, but Sofia got lucky with her topic.
Eli is more creative, which is why he started a new notebook.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts Sofia's precision with Eli's scattered approach, shows that precision leads to winning, and ends with Eli learning from the comparison by adopting a more focused method.

questions.passage: The snow had blanketed the whole town in silence. The streetlights wore halos of frost, and every bare tree held its arms up to the sky as if praying for spring.
questions.text: What literary device is used in 'every bare tree held its arms up to the sky as if praying for spring'?
options: Simile
Hyperbole
Personification
Alliteration
questions.explanation: Giving the trees human actions — holding 'arms' up and 'praying' — is personification, which attributes human qualities to nonhuman things.

questions.passage: The poem's three stanzas follow a speaker on a journey. The first stanza describes leaving home with excitement. The second stanza describes the long, lonely middle of the road where doubt creeps in. The third stanza returns to the image of home, but now the speaker sees it differently — as both a place left behind and a destination worth returning to.
questions.text: How does the structure of the three stanzas work together to develop the poem's meaning?
options: Each stanza introduces a completely unrelated topic.
The stanzas show a progression from excitement, to doubt, to a deeper understanding of home.
The third stanza simply repeats the ideas from the first stanza.
The second stanza is the most important because it has the most lines.
questions.explanation: The three stanzas form a journey arc: departure (excitement), the middle path (doubt), and return (deeper understanding), each building on the previous to develop the poem's central idea about home.

questions.passage: The story is narrated by twelve-year-old Marcus, who describes his new neighbor, Mr. Finch, as 'old and grumpy' because the man never waves back. Later, we learn that Mr. Finch had hearing loss and couldn't see the waves from his front window due to its frosted glass.
questions.text: How does Marcus's point of view as narrator affect the way events are described?
options: Marcus's narration gives the reader full and accurate information about Mr. Finch.
Marcus accurately describes Mr. Finch because he is a careful observer.
Marcus's limited perspective leads him to misunderstand Mr. Finch, coloring the reader's view until more facts are revealed.
Marcus narrates from a third-person point of view, making the story more objective.
questions.explanation: Because Marcus only sees Mr. Finch's behavior from the outside and draws incorrect conclusions, his narration shapes the reader's perception, revealing how a narrator's limited perspective can mislead.

questions.passage: The bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list in 2007, after decades of recovery efforts. The bird nearly disappeared in the mid-20th century due to hunting and the widespread use of the pesticide DDT, which thinned eagle eggshells and prevented successful hatching. After DDT was banned in 1972 and habitat protections were put in place, eagle populations began to recover steadily.
questions.text: Based on the passage, what can you infer was the MOST important factor in the bald eagle's recovery?
options: Eagles began laying more eggs once they moved to new habitats.
Removing eagles from the endangered list helped them recover.
Banning DDT and protecting habitats removed the main threats to eagle reproduction and survival.
Eagle hunting increased, which pressured the government to act.
questions.explanation: The passage identifies DDT and habitat loss as the causes of decline, and states that banning DDT and implementing habitat protections led to steady recovery, supporting this inference.

questions.passage: Exercise benefits the body in multiple ways. Regular physical activity strengthens the heart, reducing the risk of cardiovascular disease. It also builds muscle and bone density, which becomes increasingly important as people age. In addition to physical benefits, exercise has a powerful effect on mental health. Studies show that aerobic activity reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression, and regular exercise has been linked to improved sleep quality and better concentration.
questions.text: What are the TWO main ideas of this passage?
options: Exercise is fun, and everyone should do it every day.
Exercise improves physical health and also benefits mental health.
Aerobic activity is better for you than strength training.
Cardiovascular disease and depression are the most common health problems.
questions.explanation: The passage is organized around two main ideas: the physical benefits of exercise (heart, muscle, bone) and the mental health benefits (anxiety, depression, sleep, concentration).

questions.passage: The development of the transcontinental railroad transformed the relationship between the United States government, railroad companies, and Native American tribes. The government granted railroad companies vast tracts of land to lay tracks westward. This expansion displaced many Native American tribes from their homelands and disrupted traditional buffalo hunting grounds. At the same time, the railroad made it faster and cheaper to transport goods, fueling rapid economic growth in western cities.
questions.text: How did the transcontinental railroad affect different groups in different ways?
options: It benefited everyone equally by connecting the country.
It helped railroad companies and western cities economically while displacing Native American tribes.
It hurt railroad companies financially even though it helped the government.
It mainly affected farmers in the eastern United States.
questions.explanation: The passage describes how the railroad benefited companies and western cities through economic growth while simultaneously displacing Native American tribes and disrupting their way of life.

questions.passage: When tectonic plates shift suddenly, the energy released travels outward in seismic waves. The point on Earth's surface directly above the origin of an earthquake is called the epicenter. Seismologists use instruments called seismographs to detect and measure these waves.
questions.text: What does 'epicenter' mean based on the passage?
options: The instrument used to measure earthquakes.
The point underground where an earthquake begins.
The point on Earth's surface directly above where the earthquake originates.
The waves of energy that travel outward from an earthquake.
questions.explanation: The passage defines 'epicenter' directly as 'the point on Earth's surface directly above the origin of an earthquake.'

questions.passage: Account A (1920s newspaper editorial): 'The construction of the dam will bring jobs and electricity to thousands of families who have long gone without. Progress requires sacrifice, and the valley's residents who must relocate will be fairly compensated.' Account B (oral history recorded decades later): 'My grandmother told me they gave us almost nothing. We had farmed that valley for three generations. No amount of money replaces land your family has worked and loved.'
questions.text: How do the two accounts differ in their view of the dam's construction?
options: Both accounts agree the dam was a positive development.
Both accounts agree the relocations were handled unfairly.
Account A presents the dam as progress with fair compensation; Account B presents it as a loss that could not be compensated.
Account A is more reliable because it was written closer to the event.
questions.explanation: Account A frames the dam as beneficial progress with fair treatment; Account B challenges that framing, presenting the loss of ancestral land as irreplaceable, showing how perspective shapes historical accounts.

questions.passage: Cell phones should be allowed in middle school classrooms. Research from the Pew Institute found that students who can quickly look up unfamiliar terms understand lessons better. Teachers who have experimented with phone-based polling tools report higher student engagement. Additionally, learning to use technology responsibly is a key skill for future careers.
questions.text: What reasons and evidence does the author use to support the argument?
options: The author uses personal anecdotes and emotional appeals only.
The author cites research on comprehension, teacher reports of engagement, and a career-readiness argument.
The author provides statistics about how many students own phones.
The author argues that rules against phones are unfair.
questions.explanation: The author supports the argument with research findings about comprehension, teacher experience with engagement tools, and a logical argument about career skills, using multiple forms of evidence.

questions.text: In the sentence 'Oh no, I forgot my homework!' what part of speech is 'Oh no'?
options: Conjunction
Preposition
Interjection
Adverb
questions.explanation: 'Oh no' is an interjection — a word or phrase that expresses sudden emotion and is grammatically separate from the rest of the sentence.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses the present perfect tense?
options: She will finish her project by Friday.
She finished her project yesterday.
She has finished her project.
She was finishing her project.
questions.explanation: The present perfect tense uses 'has' or 'have' plus a past participle; 'She has finished her project' is in the present perfect tense.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses the past perfect tense?
options: By the time we arrived, the show already started.
By the time we arrived, the show had already started.
By the time we arrived, the show has already started.
By the time we arrived, the show will have already started.
questions.explanation: The past perfect tense uses 'had' plus a past participle to show that one past action was completed before another; 'had already started' correctly places the show's start before the arrival.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a comma to separate items in a series?
options: We need eggs milk butter and flour.
We need eggs, milk, butter and flour.
We need eggs, milk, butter, and flour.
We need, eggs, milk, butter, and flour.
questions.explanation: Items in a series are separated by commas; the Oxford (serial) comma before 'and' in 'eggs, milk, butter, and flour' is the standard correct form.

questions.text: Which revision best combines these two short sentences into one, for better style? 'The dog was big. The dog ran fast.'
options: The dog was big and the dog ran fast.
The big dog ran fast.
The dog was big, also it ran fast.
Being big, the dog was also fast.
questions.explanation: 'The big dog ran fast' combines both ideas into a single, clean sentence by using 'big' as an adjective within the main clause, eliminating wordiness.

questions.passage: After months of drought, the river had dwindled to a narrow channel barely a foot wide. Fish were stranded in shallow, disconnected pools, and the herons that usually waded there had moved upstream in search of deeper water.
questions.text: What does 'dwindled' most likely mean based on the context?
options: Flooded its banks.
Gradually decreased in size.
Changed its direction.
Frozen over completely.
questions.explanation: Clues like 'drought,' 'narrow channel barely a foot wide,' and fish stranded in shallow pools all indicate that the river had gradually decreased in size, which is the meaning of 'dwindled.'

questions.text: The Greek root 'bio' means 'life' and the suffix '-logy' means 'the study of.' What does 'biology' mean?
options: The study of the Earth's surface.
The study of living things.
The study of stars and planets.
The study of chemical reactions.
questions.explanation: Combining 'bio' (life) and '-logy' (the study of) gives 'the study of living things,' which is exactly what biology is.

questions.passage: The deadline was a monster that had been chasing Marco all week. He could feel its hot breath on his neck every time he opened his laptop.
questions.text: What figure of speech is used in 'the deadline was a monster that had been chasing Marco'?
options: Simile
Personification
Hyperbole
Metaphor
questions.explanation: Calling the deadline a monster is a metaphor — a direct comparison that says one thing IS another thing, without using 'like' or 'as.'
